newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Faulding gets set for change.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Faulding gets set for change.

text.p: Pharmaceutical group F.H. Faulding and Co Ltd was positioning itself for changes in retail pharmacy operations in Australia and pharmaceutical products worldwide, chief executive Ed Tweddell said on Wednesday.

In an interview with Reuters, Tweddell said the group's recent acquisition of the Cenovis vitamin range signified its determination, in the face of wholesaling changes, not to lose out to the inevitable deregulation of the pharmacy sector.
"To a certain extent, a lot of our actions in the old distribution business are defensive," he said.

"I think its traditional wholesaling role is going to be under a lot of pressure going forward and what we are determined to do is not lose that franchise we have - 42 percent of the retail pharmacy business in Australia," he said.
Tweddell said while the move would not be immediate, there eventually would be deregulation of pharmacies in Australia, which would create a different retail environment.
"Faulding must position itself to not only be seen as just a distributor -- if retail pharmacy drops, Faulding drops -- but to have more entrenched relationships in the whole retail push."
"I'm not saying we are going to go out...and buy a whole chain of pharmacies, but I will say we will be major players in some way in that whole interface with the customer," he said.

Tweddell said fundamental changes in pharmaceuticals worldwide, where medication choices were being influenced far more now by insurance companies than doctors, would present big opportunities for companies like Faulding.

The number of new drugs coming into the market was dropping for the first time in a generation, research and development would decline, as would the number of generic drugs, with the focus on treatments for conditions such as AIDS and heart diseases, he said.
"There are real niches of opportunity for companies like Faulding which have a basket of technology which basically make medicines better to fit in with these changes in health care."
Tweddel said Faulding next week would lodge with the United States Food and Drug Administration a major product which was "a generic to one of the biggest drugs in the U.S. market".
Faulding anticipated having to defend intellectual property claims, but the product represented "that sort of value adding which will be very much our activity over the next ten years," he said.

Tweddell said the sale of anti-cancer drugs in the United States would be a "very important part of profit contribution" for Faulding in the next five years, with most of the major anti-cancer drugs coming off patent in the U.S. in that time.
Twedell said the sales of Faulding's sustained released morphine product Kadian were going very well in the United States.
"They are beyond our expectations, the re-orders are higher than we had budgeted for and expected," he said.
